claims.title: Bull shark catch rates in shark-control gear are rising at the southernmost beaches, not just bites.
By 2050 the half-year 19°C line passes the Victorian border.
Baitfish such as mullet now run later into autumn off NSW, matching the longer bull shark season.
White shark bites on the NSW north coast peak in June–November, when humpbacks migrate past.
Cold upwelling brings white sharks close to shore.
White shark nurseries are shifting with warming water: young white sharks arrive earlier and stay longer in warm years.
The bull shark season off NSW is getting longer.
Outside Australia, bull shark bites also stop below about 19°C.
Outside Australia, tagged and recorded bull sharks are also found almost only in water of 19°C or warmer.
California's white shark incidents have moved north as the coast warmed.
Small bull sharks stay in rivers through winter; large ones leave.
Coastal bull shark bites happen within about 5 km of a river mouth, and within 3 days of more than 50 mm of rain, far more often than chance.
Heavy rain brings tiger sharks close to shore.
Western Australia's bull shark bites since 2020 came in months when the warm current down the coast was stronger than average.
Western Australia's shark bites come more often when the Indian Ocean Dipole is positive.
Bites in southern NSW are rising faster than the number of people using the beach.
Hot spells put more people and sharks in the same water at once.
Shark bites cluster around the full or new moon.
Hawaii's tiger shark bite season is becoming more concentrated in autumn as the water warms.
A large share of shark-bite deaths involved a limb wound that is survivable when bleeding is stopped within minutes.
More shark-bite victims in Australia survive than in past decades.
Shark nets reduce bull shark bites at the beaches they cover.
SMART drumlines would catch more bull sharks if they were also set at dawn, dusk or night.
Most animals caught in Queensland's shark-control gear are not tiger, bull or white sharks.
Human greenhouse gas emissions, not natural swings, account for most of the extra months the sea off Sydney now spends at 19°C or warmer.
Growing seal and sea lion colonies bring white sharks to nearby swimming beaches.
There are more young bull sharks in the southern nurseries, not only the same sharks ranging further south.
Other warm-water species off eastern Australia are being recorded further south at about the same pace as the 19°C line.
Turtle movements predict when tiger sharks arrive.
Sharks off NSW are eating more tropical fish as tropical species move south.
Shark feeding and cage diving keep sharks near those sites longer, without raising bites at nearby beaches.
When a beach is closed after a sighting, or the water turns murky after rain, most people stay out of the water.
Drones with infrared or multi-band cameras spot shark-sized targets in water under 1.5 m visibility at least twice as often as standard drones.
A tourniquet built into a surf leash stops blood flow to the leg as well as a standard medical tourniquet, when an untrained surfer applies it in under a minute.
Shark-bite victims at beaches with a bleeding kit close by, or a patrol on duty, have bleeding controlled sooner and survive more often.
The beaches gaining warm-water months fastest are among the least prepared: fewer bleeding kits, fewer patrol days and longer ambulance times.
Bite-resistant wetsuits reduce injuries from bull shark bites, not just white and tiger shark bites, and reduce severe bleeding in real incidents.
Lights that break up a surfer's outline from below, proven on seal-shaped decoys, also reduce white shark approaches to real surfboards, and work for bull and tiger sharks.
In the days before a bite, tagged sharks were detected at nearby listening stations more often than usual.
Rivers that drain cleared, farmed or built-up land bring more bull sharks to their mouths when they run high.
Shark bites cluster near boat ramps and fish-cleaning tables, where fish scraps go into the water.
Canal estates and built-up estuaries hold bull sharks for more of the year than natural estuaries do.
Heavy fishing of baitfish such as mullet near the coast pushes sharks to hunt closer to the beaches.
Estuaries that have lost more of their mangroves and seagrass hold fewer young bull sharks.
